hops.afterHeading: The map, and three ways to build it
hops.title: Make your own thumb disappear
hops.text: Hold both thumbs up at arm's length. Close your left eye, look at your left thumbnail, and slowly slide your right thumb to the right, nudging it a little up or down. About fifteen degrees out, its tip vanishes. That is your blind spot, where ganglion cell axons gather to leave the retina as the optic nerve and there are no photoreceptors. Where the optic nerve exits the retina fixes that gap's place, and ordered mapping preserves it in the brain. You see no dark hole, though: your visual system fills it with the background, and in macaques, neurons in the blind-spot part of V1 respond when it does.

sources.citation: Miller, Wallis, Bex & Arnold, Curr. Biol. 25:R747 (2015)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a desk with one eye closed, holding both thumbs out at arm's length.
image.caption: The optic nerve's exit has no photoreceptors, so each eye has a blind spot at a fixed place.

hops.title: Eph and ephrin slopes sort the mouse gut lining
hops.text: Mice use opposing Eph and ephrin slopes to sort the cells lining their small intestine. New lining cells are born in pockets called crypts. EphB2 is highest near the bottom of each crypt and fades toward the top, where ephrin-B1 is highest, and EphB3 sits in the cells at the base. Cells that absorb nutrients or release mucus or hormones travel up toward the gut surface. Paneth cells go the other way, down to the crypt base. In 2002, Eduard Batlle, Hans Clevers and colleagues found that in adult mice lacking EphB3, Paneth cells were scattered through the crypts, with a few reaching the villi.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Soft folded tissue ridges with deep blue cells tucked at the bottom of the pockets and pale gold cells along the upper ridges.
image.caption: EphB and ephrin-B signals help sort mouse gut cells, and EphB3 helps position Paneth cells at the crypt base.

hops.title: Barn owls wearing sideways prism glasses
hops.text: A barn owl's optic tectum holds two topographic maps in register, one of sight and one of sound location, aligned so a rustle in the dark and a glimpse of a mouse point to the same spot. In 1998, Michael Brainard and Eric Knudsen fitted young barn owls with prism spectacles that shifted their view twenty-three degrees to one side. Gradually, visual experience pulled the tectum's sound map sideways to match the shifted sight. That same year, Knudsen showed that adult owls adapted little to a large, unfamiliar shift introduced all at once, but could recover one they had learned as juveniles even after a long break.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A barn owl on a mossy branch wearing tiny round prism glasses, tilting its head toward a leaf.
image.caption: Young owls in prism glasses shifted their tectum's sound map to match their shifted sight.

audio.title: Letters on the Brain, Upside-Down Goggles, and a Frog Toxin in the Dark
audio.transcript: Here are three places where the brain's visual map turns up in real life. First, a prosthetic that writes straight onto the map. The long-standing plan for restoring sight with electrodes on visual cortex was to flash small spots that would combine like pixels on a screen. When several electrodes were stimulated at once, though, the spots often merged into larger patches that obscured the intended shapes; in one participant, five electrodes stimulated together produced only two large patches. In twenty twenty, Michael Beauchamp, Daniel Yoshor and their team tried something different. They leaned on the fact that visual cortex holds an orderly spatial map of the world, and swept tiny pulses of current from one electrode to the next, tracing letter shapes across the brain's surface the way you might trace a letter on a friend's palm. Blind volunteers recognized the traced shapes. One picked out three letter-like shapes correctly about ninety-two percent of the time at thirty a minute, and in a faster test told upward from downward lines at about eighty-six a minute. The map was still there, waiting to be read in order. Second, once that map is wired in, it is stubborn. There is a popular claim that if you wear upside-down prism goggles for a week, your brain flips the picture back right side up. Would the picture really turn upright, or would people simply get better at moving through an upside-down world? In nineteen ninety-nine, David Linden and his colleagues tested it. Four volunteers wore inverting spectacles for six to ten days and were scanned with functional M R I. They quickly adapted their movements, yet none reported seeing the world upright again. The scans found no sign that their early visual cortex had flipped its map. Their movements adapted on top of a map that stayed put. Third, how does a map get sharp before an animal ever opens its eyes? Molecular slopes guide axons toward the right regions, and while those connections are forming, the retina runs its own test pattern in the dark. In nineteen ninety-one, Markus Meister, Carla Shatz and colleagues recorded spontaneous activity in isolated retinas from newborn ferrets and fetal cats. Neighboring ganglion cells fired together in slow waves several hundred micrometers wide, rolling across the retina at about one hundred micrometers per second, once every minute or two. To interfere with those waves, neuroscientists later borrowed a frog toxin. Epibatidine was first found in nineteen seventy-four in the skin of an Ecuadorian poison frog now called Epipedobates anthonyi, and its structure was worked out in nineteen ninety-two. It is far too toxic to use as a painkiller, and it acts on the same nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that drive early retinal waves. In a study published in two thousand nine, Alexandra Rebsam, Timothy Petros and Carol Mason used epibatidine in both eyes of newborn mice to disrupt early retinal waves during their first week. Later, in the visual relay of the thalamus, axons from the two eyes failed to sort properly into their own zones. Slopes give axons their neighborhood; waves in the dark help sort and sharpen what the slopes started.
